findings.headline: Challenges in delivery of approved savings targets during 2025/26 require enhanced monitoring arrangements in 2026/27
findings.detail: Monthly Directorate Budget Boards identified 'challenges in the delivery of approved and brought forward saving targets during 2025/26'. To address this, the council is strengthening 'arrangements to monitor progress and identify risks and challenges to delivery' in 2026/27, with monthly monitoring led by Service Directors or Corporate Directors. Directorate expenditure control panels are being continued to manage cost pressures.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver planned savings in 2025/26 indicates budget assumptions may be optimistic or that operational pressures exceed forecasts; track record of savings delivery affects confidence in 2026/27 budget and future financial sustainability plans.
findings.figures: Specific quantum of 2025/26 savings shortfall not disclosed in this statement
findings.quote: Monthly Directorate Budget Boards have provided improved oversight of key cost pressures, delivery of the capital programme and challenges in the delivery of approved and brought forward saving targets during 2025/26

findings.headline: Council identified unquantified future funding gap requiring new financial strategy from April 2026
findings.detail: The governance statement identifies 'Activity to develop specific actions and milestones as part of the council's Future Financial Strategy will be a key focus from April 2026 to close the estimated funding gap in future years and protect the council's future financial sustainability.' The council set a balanced budget for 2026/27 but acknowledges a structural gap beyond that year that requires a credible financial strategy to close.
findings.matters: An unquantified multi-year funding gap suggests structural budget pressures beyond cyclical pressures; the timing and magnitude of this gap will determine whether the council needs to cut services, increase borrowing, or deploy reserves.
findings.figures: Estimated funding gap in future years (quantum not disclosed)
findings.quote: Activity to develop specific actions and milestones as part of the council's Future Financial Strategy will be a key focus from April 2026 to close the estimated funding gap in future years and protect the council's future financial sustainability.

findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit of £36.3m creates £3.6m balance-sheet liability when statutory override expires in March 2028
findings.detail: The council's Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit is £36.3m at 31 March 2026, driven by £16.3m overspend in High Needs Block. Currently treated as unusable reserve under statutory override expiring March 2028. When override ends, 90% (£32.7m) should be covered by High Needs Stability Grant subject to DfE approval of a Local SEND Reform Plan due 19 June 2026, but the remaining 10% (£3.6m) becomes a direct liability on the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: £3.6m contingent liability will crystallise in three years, reducing financial flexibility and potentially affecting borrowing capacity; ongoing High Needs demand pressures require the council to deliver savings to offset SEND costs, creating competing financial pressures.
findings.figures: DSG cumulative deficit £36.3m; High Needs Block overspend £16.3m; future liability £3.6m from March 2028; required High Needs Stability Grant £32.7m (subject to DfE approval)
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, the council's Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) cumulative deficit is £36.3 million following a £16.3 million overspend within the High Needs Block... with the remaining balance of £3.6 million (10%) to be a liability of the council once the statutory override period ends in March 2028.

findings.headline: Council secured £55.0 million in new long-term borrowing during the final quarter at 4.83% for a 10-year term.
findings.detail: In the final quarter of 2025/26, the council undertook significant new borrowing of £55.0 million on a 10-year repayment term at 4.83%. This borrowing decision came as section 2.1 notes that 'PWLB rates are based on gilt yields, which rose materially in March 2026', indicating the council locked in borrowing at a time of rising interest rates.
findings.matters: A major borrowing decision at rising rates indicates urgent liquidity needs and locks the council into 10 years of payments at 4.83%, a material commitment affecting revenue budget sustainability.
findings.figures: £55.0 million new borrowing at 4.83% for 10-year repayment term
findings.quote: the council held long-term borrowing of £185.1 million; this includes a new long-term loan of £55.0 million which has been secured during the final quarter of the financial year (10-year repayment term at 4.83% interest).

findings.headline: The council holds £145.7 million of internal borrowing, financing 44% of its Capital Financing Requirement from reserves rather than external debt.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) at 31 March 2026 is £330.8 million, but actual long-term borrowing is only £185.1 million, leaving £145.7 million financed from internal resources. This means the council is financing nearly half of its capital requirement from cash reserves rather than external borrowing. The paper explicitly flags this position as 'significant internal borrowing'.
findings.matters: High internal borrowing indicates reserve depletion to finance capital, reduces external debt headroom, and affects liquidity and financial flexibility for lenders assessing future debt capacity.
findings.figures: CFR £330.8 million; long-term borrowing £185.1 million; internal borrowing £145.7 million (44% of CFR)
findings.quote: The council's CFR at 31 March 2026 is £330.8 million, which demonstrates that the Council has significant internal borrowing when compared to the actual long-term borrowing (excluding PFI liabilities) of £185.1 million.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure came in at £86.0 million against a budget of £155.2 million, a 44% underspend.
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £155.2 million in capital expenditure for 2025/26 but delivered only £86.0 million. Section 4.5 attributes this to 'slippage in the capital investment budget spend'. This represents a significant variance that may indicate either planning overoptimism or delivery capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Substantial capital underspend signals difficulty executing the council's investment programme, which affects strategic delivery and debt management plans that lenders rely on.
findings.figures: £155.2 million budgeted, £86.0 million actual spend; represents 44% underspend
findings.quote: the outturn spend for the financial year 2025/26 of £86.0 million is shown against a Prudential indicator value approved in the Treasury Management Strategy of £155.2 million.

findings.headline: Employment Land and Incubation Space development delayed by planning and contractor issues
findings.detail: Employment Land & Incubation Space in Market Towns shows an outturn of £1.047m against a budget of £3.961m, a variance of -£2.914m. Works started later than planned (January/February 2026) due to 'programme adjustment by contractor to account for planning infrastructure approvals'.
findings.matters: Economic development projects are material to business rates forecasting and growth strategy. A £2.9m delay in a £14.6m multi-year scheme indicates planning and contractor coordination challenges that may affect the council's economic development pipeline and associated revenue assumptions.
findings.figures: £3.961m budget vs £1.047m outturn; -£2.914m variance; £14.648m total scheme budget
findings.quote: Spend re-profiled into 26/27 due to works starting on-site later than planned, Jan/Feb '26 following programme adjustment by contractor to account for planning infrastructure approvals.

findings.headline: Integrated Wetlands schemes deemed unviable mid-delivery, funding reallocation pending
findings.detail: The Integrated Wetlands programme shows a variance of -£349k with the council reporting that 'Dilwyn wetland and Lucton PTP schemes are proving to be unviable for delivery and funding is likely to be reallocated pending decisions in 26/27'.
findings.matters: Mid-project scheme abandonment indicates environmental and technical due diligence was insufficient at project approval. The pending reallocation decision suggests ongoing governance uncertainty and capital deployment risk.
findings.figures: £1.686m budget vs £1.337m outturn; -£349k variance
findings.quote: Dilwyn wetland and Lucton PTP schemes are proving to be unviable for delivery and funding is likely to be reallocated pending decisions in 26/27

findings.headline: Hereford Western Bypass Phase 1 land acquisition significantly more complex than planned
findings.detail: The Western Bypass Phase 1 shows an outturn of £1.026m against a budget of £2.1m, a variance of -£1.074m. The council acknowledges the original land purchase programme 'did not fully reflect the extent of the role of the pre-construction services contractor', particularly regarding timing of land vacation.
findings.matters: This is a major transport infrastructure project. Underestimated complexity in land acquisition suggests planning weaknesses and raises the risk that the total project cost may exceed current forecasts. Land acquisition delays typically cascade through construction schedules.
findings.figures: £2.1m budget vs £1.026m outturn; -£1.074m variance
findings.quote: The original land purchase programme did not fully reflect the extent of the role of the pre-construction services contractor in the process, particularly in relation to how and when land is vacated

findings.headline: Shire Hall Improvement Works completely paused pending strategic option review
findings.detail: The Shire Hall Improvement Works budget of £250k shows zero outturn, indicating the entire project is on hold. The council states delays are occurring 'while an option review has taken place', meaning no activity or expenditure during the year.
findings.matters: A complete project freeze on major council estate works suggests either strategic uncertainty or governance challenges in property investment decisions. This can affect operational efficiency and signals decision-making delays at senior level.
findings.figures: £250k budgeted; £0 spent; -£250k variance
findings.quote: There have been delays to the project while an option review has taken place

findings.headline: Waste transformation delayed by government funding announcement uncertainty
findings.detail: The waste capital programme shows an outturn of £397k against a budget of £5.193m, a variance of -£4.796m (92% underspend). The delay to the new food waste service is explicitly attributed to government funding announcement delays. The garden waste service has had bin purchases cut to 50% pending subscription growth.
findings.matters: Government funding uncertainty for environmental services creates operational and revenue risk. The garden waste service is now constrained by subscription levels, creating income volatility that affects service sustainability and the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £4.796m capital variance; garden waste bins reduced to 50% pending subscriptions
findings.quote: Expenditure for introduction of new food waste service delayed due to Government funding announcement delays and expenditure on purchase of bins for garden waste service reduced in this financial year to half until subscriptions increase sufficiently to order more.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered £27.8m below budget due to widespread project delays
findings.detail: The council's capital programme outturn was £85.991m against a current budget of £113.820m, creating a variance of -£27.830m. Of this, £25.015m is attributed to projects delayed into 2026/27, and £2.814k to projects delivering under budget. This represents a 24% underspend across the entire capital programme.
findings.matters: A capital programme underspend of this magnitude suggests systematic capital delivery and planning challenges. For lenders, this indicates potential governance weaknesses in project management and raises questions about the council's ability to execute capital projects to schedule.
findings.figures: £27.830m variance (24% underspend); £25.015m from delays; £113.820m budget vs £85.991m outturn
findings.quote: Projects likely to be delayed into 26/27, some with no decisions yet made on spend, others with delays in delivery. -25,015 Project to deliver under budget or not spend full grant allocation -2,814

findings.headline: The Budget Resilience Reserve was drawn down mid-year (£1.8m) and repaid by year-end (£1.4m), indicating tight cash management
findings.detail: Adult Social Care underspent by £1.8m through use of the Budget Resilience Reserve (to manage demand pressures), but this was subsequently repaid (£1.4m through Children & Young People). This pattern suggests the council needed to access reserves mid-year to manage cash flow but was able to rebuild them.
findings.matters: While reserves were repaid, the need to draw them down mid-year signals tight month-to-month cash management and reduced financial flexibility; if this pattern repeats, it erodes the council's buffer for unexpected costs or revenue shocks
findings.figures: £1.8m drawn; £1.4m repaid; net use £0.4m
findings.quote: £1.8m underspend - Use of Budget Resilience Reserve

findings.headline: Children's residential placements overspent by £1.2m, the largest variance in the Children & Young People directorate
findings.detail: The Children & Young People directorate overspent by £1.2m specifically on Residential Placements (budget £42.0m, outturn £43.2m), making this the single largest overspend in that directorate despite underspends elsewhere.
findings.matters: Residential placement costs for children indicate pressure in safeguarding and family support; these are difficult-to-control costs once a child enters the system and often indicate rising per-placement costs or case complexity
findings.figures: £1.2m overspend on Residential Placements; Children & Young People directorate total underspend £1.2m
findings.quote: £1.2m overspend - Residential Placements

findings.headline: Savings plans from 2024/25 were not delivered and added £1.5m to 2025/26 costs
findings.detail: The Central budget shows £1.5m overspend driven by '2024/25 c/fwd outstanding Saving Plans not delivered'. This indicates efficiency savings targeted in the previous year were not achieved and their cost impact carried into the current year.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings plans signal execution risk and governance concerns; if a council cannot deliver planned efficiency savings in one year, it suggests structural challenges in delivery capacity that affect confidence in future financial planning
findings.figures: £1.5m overspend from prior-year undelivered savings
findings.quote: £1.5m overspend - 2024/25 c/fwd outstanding Saving Plans not delivered

findings.headline: Home to School and SEN transport exceeded budget by £2.6m, the largest variance in Economy & Environment
findings.detail: Residential Services for SEN & Home to School Transport overspent by £2.6m, making this the largest single overspend in that directorate (budget £12.7m, outturn £15.4m). This was not offset by other underspends and is a material variance.
findings.matters: Transport costs are contractual and statutory once committed; a £2.6m overspend indicates cost inflation or demand pressures that will likely persist and are difficult to control
findings.figures: £2.6m overspend; 21% variance on a £12.7m budget
findings.quote: £2.6m overspend - Home to School/College & SEN Transport

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspent by £6.5m due to increased demand for residential, nursing, homecare and personal budgets
findings.detail: The Community Wellbeing directorate's largest variance is a £6.5m overspend explicitly attributed to increased demand for Adult Social Care Residential, Nursing, Homecare and Personal Budgets. This is the single largest variance in the council's budget and was partly offset by drawing down the Budget Resilience Reserve (£1.8m).
findings.matters: Demand-driven social care overspends signal demographic and cost pressures that typically recur; this materially affects the council's financial trajectory and is the type of pressure that erodes financial flexibility year-on-year
findings.figures: £6.5m overspend; Community Wellbeing directorate total overspend £3.7m
findings.quote: £6.5m overspend - Increase in demand for Adult Social Care - Residential, Nursing, Homecare and Personal Budgets

findings.headline: Community Wellbeing and SEND/home-to-school transport overspends driven by demand growth and cost inflation with no clear ceiling
findings.detail: Community Wellbeing overspent by £3.7m and SEND/home-to-school transport by £2.6m, totalling £6.3m of directorate overspends. The council cites 'increasing complexity of need and intensity of care for the county's ageing population, increased demand for temporary accommodation and increasing demand and costs in Special Educational Needs.' Planned 2026/27 mitigations include market engagement for care contracts and an in-house transport model, but these are uncertain and may not arrest the underlying trend.
findings.matters: These are non-discretionary, demand-led budgets in which cost pressures are structural, not cyclical. If the council cannot control costs in these areas, it will face repeated reliance on reserves and savings from other services, or borrowing to fund current spending.
findings.figures: Community Wellbeing overspend £3.7m; SEN/home-to-school transport overspend £2.6m; home-to-school transport budget £12.7m with outturn £15.3m
findings.quote: The council has experienced continuing cost pressures in 2025/26 as a result of increasing complexity of need and intensity of care for the county's ageing population, increased demand for temporary accommodation and increasing demand and costs in Special Educational Needs (SEN) and home to school transport budgets.

findings.headline: Budget Resilience Reserve depleted to £1.0m after transfers, down from £7.0m, leaving minimal contingency
findings.detail: The Budget Resilience Reserve was drawn down by £1.8m in 2025/26 to offset overspends, reducing it from £7.0m to £5.2m. The approved 2026/27 budget requires a further £4.2m transfer to a Contract Inflation Fund, leaving only £1.0m as working contingency for future pressures. This is a material reduction in financial flexibility and suggests tightening resilience to shocks.
findings.matters: Reserves below 1% of spend are inadequate for a council facing demand volatility in social care and SEND. The transfer of most remaining reserves to inflation management leaves no buffer for variances or unexpected costs, increasing financial risk.
findings.figures: Budget Resilience Reserve: £7.0m (start) → £5.2m (end of 2025/26) → £1.0m (after 2026/27 transfer); transfer to Contract Inflation Fund £4.2m; total draw in 2025/26 £1.8m
findings.quote: This transfer reduces the Budget Resilience Reserve balance from £7.0 million to £5.2 million at 31 March 2026; of which £1.0 million will be retained in this reserve and carried forward to provide resilience against budget pressures in future years. As per the approved 2026/27 revenue budget, £4.2 million will be transferred on 1 April 2026 to support the centrally held Contract Inflation Fund.

findings.headline: Savings plan delivered at only 84%; £2.6m of £15.8m target not achieved, with £11.9m from prior years still incomplete
findings.detail: The council delivered £13.2m of £15.8m savings target (84%), missing by £2.6m. Additionally, £11.9m of savings from previous financial years that were carried forward remain incomplete—only £9.3m was delivered recurrently. Community & Wellbeing delivered only £2.3m of £3.2m target (£0.9m shortfall); council-wide savings only £5.9m of £7.3m. This pattern suggests systemic execution issues with planned financial improvements.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to land savings targets on this scale indicates the financial strategy may not be deliverable. A lender needs confidence that planned savings underpin future budgets; missing 16% of targets, combined with prior-year carryforwards, suggests structural imbalance.
findings.figures: 2025/26 savings delivered £13.2m of £15.8m (84%); not delivered £2.6m; prior-year carryforward £11.9m with only £9.3m delivered recurrently; Community & Wellbeing shortfall £0.9m; council-wide shortfall £1.4m
findings.quote: The total value of savings delivered in 2025/26 is £13.2 million (84%) of the combined target for the year.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs deficit increased by £16.3m in year to £36.3m cumulative, with ongoing growth trajectory
findings.detail: The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grew from £20.0m at start of year to £36.3m at year-end, driven by £16.3m overspend in the High Needs Block. While the government will cover 90% (£32.7m) through a High Needs Stability Grant, the council remains liable for £3.6m from 2028 onwards. The deficit management plan continues but deficits are growing faster than mitigations.
findings.matters: A growing DSG deficit at this scale signals structural SEND costs the council cannot manage within normal budget and will need to fund through borrowing or reserves for years. It directly affects medium-term borrowing requirement and debt sustainability.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £36.3m (up from £20.0m); annual High Needs overspend £16.3m in 2025/26; council liability £3.6m from 2028; grant (pending approval) £32.7m (90%)
findings.quote: The outturn position for 2025/26 is an overspend of £16.3 million within the High Needs Block of the DSG, increasing the cumulative deficit to £36.3 million at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: The council is anticipating significant additional borrowing in the final quarter to finance the ongoing DSG deficit.
findings.detail: The document explicitly forecasts that significant further borrowing will be undertaken in Q4 of 2025/26, specifically driven by the ongoing impact of financing the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit. At 31 December 2025, the council held £135.2m in long-term borrowing against a Capital Financing Requirement of £320.6m, demonstrating substantial internal borrowing of approximately £185.4m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's cash flow pressures and structural funding challenges. DSG deficit financing indicates ongoing budget pressures requiring additional borrowing to cover in-year shortfalls, reducing future flexibility and revealing tighter financial headroom.
findings.figures: Long-term borrowing £135.2m; Capital Financing Requirement £320.6m; DSG deficit financing driving Q4 borrowing need
findings.quote: It is anticipated that significant further borrowing will be undertaken in the final quarter of the financial year, due to actual expenditure within the capital programme and the ongoing impact of financing the DSG deficit.

findings.headline: Community Capital Grants Scheme showing £1.05m underspend due to revised payment schedules from recipients
findings.detail: The scheme allocated £1.376m budget but only £326k forecast spend, an underspend of £1.05m. The reason is 'Revised payment schedules have been received from grant recipients now the grants have been awarded.' Recipient organisations are drawing down slower than planned.
findings.matters: When council grants to external bodies don't draw down as forecast, it suggests either weak project planning by recipients or lack of demand. This indicates the council's ability to deploy community grants may be weaker than expected.
findings.figures: Scheme budget £1,376k, forecast £326k, underspend £1,050k

findings.headline: Programme is heavily dependent on £136m of discretionary government grants awarded since February 2025

findings.matters: A capital programme that relies this heavily on discretionary grants is vulnerable to government spending announcements. If grants are withdrawn, the council cannot complete these projects without borrowing. This adds medium-term financing risk.

findings.headline: Strategic option reviews pausing major council property projects (Shire Hall, Library relocation)
findings.detail: Both Shire Hall Improvement Works (£250k full underspend, forecast £0) and Stronger Towns Library relocation (£90k underspend) cite 'delays to the project while an option review has taken place.' These are not tactical slips; they are strategic pauses suggesting council uncertainty about direction.
findings.matters: Option reviews suggest unresolved governance decisions at senior level. When two major projects stall simultaneously for strategic reasons, it indicates the council is reconsidering its capital priorities mid-year, which adds execution risk.

findings.detail: Housing acquisitions delayed needing 'phosphate mitigation credit' (Buttercross project), Hereford City Centre Transport Package initially assumed 'requirement to remove contaminated soil from site' (now not needed), Integrated Wetlands delayed on 'purchasing the Dilwyn site.' These are environmental/regulatory hurdles not initially accounted for.
findings.matters: Environmental compliance is increasing in cost and complexity. Repeated surprises on what is needed (phosphate mitigation, contaminated land) show weak environmental due diligence upfront. For a lender, this signals project delivery risk and potential cost overruns.

findings.headline: Waste service rollout stalled by Government funding announcement delays; garden waste subscriptions underperforming
findings.detail: The waste programme (£3,311k underspend) cites 'Government funding announcement delays' for the new food waste service and bin purchase for garden waste 'reduced in this financial year to half until subscriptions increase sufficiently to order more.' This shows both external dependency and revenue model risk.
findings.matters: A revenue-funded service that depends on subscription uptake is struggling to hit targets. This suggests either pricing/uptake issues or service design problems. Government funding uncertainty adds further risk to a council that already faces waste management cost pressures.
findings.figures: Waste budget underspend £3,311k against planned £5,193k spending
findings.quote: Expenditure for introduction of new food waste service delayed due to Government funding announcement delays and expenditure on purchase of bins for garden waste service reduced in this financial year to half until subscriptions increase sufficiently to order more.

findings.detail: The original approved budget for 2025/26 was £155,247k, but this was reprof­iled down by £60,332k before the start of the year. This is not simply timing; it represents a 39% reduction in the year's planned capital spend against what was formally approved.
findings.matters: A £60m downward revision after Council approval suggests significant planning uncertainty or external constraint. For a lender, this indicates the council struggles to maintain a reliable capital plan.

findings.detail: The Q3 forecast of £93,968k is £21,150k below the current budget of £115,118k. The council attributes £18.5m to projects delayed into 26/27 and £2.6m to projects delivering under budget. This represents a material slip in execution.
findings.matters: An 18% underspend signals either overly optimistic budgeting or execution challenges that could indicate longer-term capital delivery risk. A lender needs to know if the council can actually deliver its investment programme on schedule.

findings.detail: General Fund Housing temporary accommodation is running £0.3m over budget at Q3, adding to demand pressures already visible in Adult Social Care.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are demand-driven and volatile; this adds a third structural pressure to the revenue account alongside ASC and SEN

findings.detail: The council faces a £0.6m overspend in Strategic Finance: £0.4m driven by increased whole-council insurance premiums and £0.2m by rising banking fees (attributed to higher volume of online transactions). These are structural cost increases.

findings.detail: The council is carrying forward £1.4m of savings targets from 2024/25 that are explicitly marked as 'at risk' of delivery. This indicates the council missed its prior-year savings targets and cannot reliably deliver planned reductions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can deliver on its savings commitments; this signals either capability issues or that the easy savings have been exhausted

findings.detail: SEN Transport is running £2.1m over budget at Q3. This is a second structural demand pressure on the revenue account, driven by increased need for transport provision for children with special educational needs.
findings.matters: Like ASC, transport demand for SEND children grows faster than budgets; a £2.1m overspend mid-year suggests a full-year pressure of £2.8-3m if the trend continues

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand overspend of £6.4m driving the council into deficit
findings.detail: The largest single variance in the council's budget is a £6.4m overspend in Adult Social Care, driven by increased demand across residential care, nursing care, homecare and personal budgets. At Q3, this overspend already represents a material risk to the year-end position and indicates structural demand pressures the council cannot easily control.
findings.matters: ASC is demand-driven and typically grows ahead of funding; at £6.4m overspend mid-year, the council is tracking to a significant full-year deficit in this area unless further mitigation is found

findings.quote: £6.4m overspend - Increase in demand for Adult Social Care - Residential, Nursing, Homecare and Personal Budgets

findings.headline: Council deliberately under-borrowed, betting on long-term interest rates falling
findings.detail: Rather than borrowing now to fund its full capital financing requirement, the council is using cash reserves as a temporary bridge. This is an explicit tactical bet that longer-term borrowing rates (currently 5.8% for 25-year PWLB loans) will fall.
findings.matters: If long-term rates do not fall as forecast, or if the council faces an unexpected need for cash, it will be forced to borrow at less favorable rates or face refinancing risk. This concentrates market/rate risk.
findings.figures: PWLB 25-year rate currently 5.8%; forecast base rate falls from 3.75% (Dec 2025) to 3.25% by end of 2026/27
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as medium and longer term dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels.

findings.headline: Gross debt-to-CFR ratio rising from 58% to 85% in four years
findings.detail: The ratio of total gross debt to the capital financing requirement (the measure of underlying borrowing need) climbs sharply from 58% in 2024/25 to 85% by 2028/29. While remaining below the 100% prudential code ceiling, the trajectory shows accelerating leverage.
findings.matters: Rising leverage relative to underlying capital need indicates the council is taking on debt at an accelerating rate. This trajectory is material to refinancing risk and debt sustainability.
findings.quote: The ratio of gross debt to CFR is below 100% for each of the disclosed years, confirming that gross debt does not exceed CFR, and that the council is operating within the parameters as set out by the Prudential Code.

findings.headline: Debt servicing costs rising to 15% of revenue budget by 2028/29
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs (interest + MRP) to net revenue stream is forecast to climb from 10% in 2024/25 to 15% by 2028/29. Absolute financing costs rise from £20.6m to £35.2m.
findings.matters: As debt servicing consumes more of the revenue budget, discretionary spending and service capacity contract. At 15%, the council is at the top end of sustainable debt servicing burden.
findings.quote: The calculated ratios of between 10% and 15% confirm that the council's borrowing is currently considered to be affordable.

findings.headline: Council borrowing forecast to grow 66% in 18 months
findings.detail: Total loan debt expected to grow from £135.5m (October 2025) to £225.8m by March 2027. This £90.3m increase in 18 months is driven by expanded capital spending and DSG funding, representing material acceleration in leverage.
findings.matters: Lenders assess credit risk partly through leverage trajectory. A 66% debt increase over 18 months is material and shows the council is significantly increasing its balance-sheet risk.
findings.quote: This is expected to increase to £225.8 million by 31 March 2027

findings.headline: Council now borrowing specifically to fund Dedicated Schools Grant deficit
findings.detail: £19.9m of the £64.4m new borrowing planned for 2026/27 is explicitly to fund the DSG deficit, a national schools funding shortfall. This signals the council's revenue budget cannot absorb schools funding pressures and it must resort to capital borrowing.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether budget pressures are temporary cyclical issues or structural problems. DSG deficits are known to be recurring and persistent — borrowing to cover them rather than absorbing them in the budget signals structural revenue stress.
findings.figures: £19.9 million DSG borrowing; £64.4 million total new borrowing in 2026/27
findings.quote: additional prudential borrowing to fund DSG of £19.9 million

findings.headline: Interest rate assumptions of 4.9% declining to 4.6%, with £2.1m exposure per 1% movement
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes capital borrowing costs at 4.9% for 2026/27 declining to 4.6% by 2029/30. A 1% movement in interest rates would have a full-year impact of £2.1m on the council's finances. Given economic volatility and the council's capital programme financing needs, this represents material downside risk.
findings.matters: Lenders care about debt servicing capacity. A 1% rise in rates would add c£2m to annual costs, worsening the already substantial funding gaps.
findings.figures: Assumed rates 4.9%, 4.7%, 4.6%, 4.6% for years 2026/27 through 2029/30; 1% movement impact = ±£2.1m
findings.quote: Capital borrowing rates of 4.9%, 4.7%, 4.6% and 4.6% have been assumed in respect of financing the Capital Programme over the next 4 years respectively.

findings.headline: £10.4 million of one-off reserve uses in 2026/27 will need permanent funding from 2027/28
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget uses £3.2m from the Business Rates Risk Reserve and establishes a £7.1m Contract Inflation Fund. The MTFS explicitly states these one-time drawdowns will 'need to be funded recurrently from 2027/28', adding to the structural funding gap. Additionally, Q2 2025/26 forecast shows £2.8m draw on the Budget Resilience Reserve, reducing reserves available for future risk management.
findings.matters: These one-off uses mask the true underlying deficit. Once exhausted, they crystallise as additional permanent pressures, worsening the already substantial 2027/28 gap.
findings.figures: £3.2 million Business Rates Risk Reserve; £7.1 million Contract Inflation Fund; £2.8 million Budget Resilience Reserve draw (Q2 2025/26)
findings.quote: The MTFS assumes that the proposed use of reserves in 2026/27 (£3.2 million of the Business Rates Risk Reserve and £7.1 million establishment of the Contract Inflation Fund) will need to be funded recurrently from 2027/28.

findings.headline: DSG deficit statutory protection expires March 2028 with no confirmed solution
findings.detail: The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is held as an unusable reserve (quarantined from the general fund) until 31 March 2028. Government has promised a Schools White Paper confirming SEND funding reform, but this has not yet been confirmed. The risk register flags this as 'high' likelihood and notes it 'cannot currently be mitigated'. After March 2028, the deficit could hit the general fund.
findings.matters: This is an external timing bomb: the council has no control over whether government extends the override or provides funded solutions, but faces potential material hit to its balance sheet in less than two years.
findings.figures: Statutory override expires 31 March 2028; cumulative amount not stated in this extract
findings.quote: The council awaits confirmation of adequate funding for SEND services in Herefordshire and a real solution to address the cumulative DSG deficit at the end of the statutory override period in March 2028 to minimise the impact on the council's financial position.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget depends on delivery of £20 million in planned savings
findings.detail: The balanced 2026/27 budget relies entirely on achieving £20m in savings across all directorates. The risk register identifies 'non-delivery of savings required to balance the budget' as a medium-likelihood, high-impact risk. If savings do not materialise, the council will need to draw reserves or cut spending mid-year.
findings.matters: Execution risk on savings directly determines whether the council can balance without unplanned reserve depletion or in-year budget cuts.
findings.figures: £20.0 million total savings; breakdown by directorate: Community Wellbeing £7.4m, Children & Young People £3.3m, Economy & Environment £7.2m, Corporate £1.5m, Central £0.5m
findings.quote: The MTFS proposes a balanced revenue budget which totals £234.1 million for 2026/27; achieved by a 4.99% increase in council tax and planned savings of £20.0 million.

findings.headline: Business rates reset reduces budgeted income from £47.6m to £31.5m, a structural £16m cut
findings.detail: The 2026 reset of the Business Rates Retention Scheme produces a permanent reduction in business rates income. While £11.5m has been rolled into Revenue Support Grant (compensation for baseline changes), the net structural change leaves the council with materially lower own-source tax revenue going forward.
findings.matters: This is a permanent reduction in the council's discretionary revenue base, making it harder to balance budgets without service cuts or further council tax increases.
findings.figures: £47.6 million (2025/26) vs £31.5 million (2026/27); comprises £30.1m baseline funding level and £1.4m surplus; £11.5m rolled into RSG
findings.quote: This budget is significantly lower than the £47.6 million budgeted income in 2025/26 as a result of the system reforms as part of which £11.5 million has been rolled into the Revenue Support Grant for 2026/27

findings.headline: Projected funding gap of £83.4 million across the MTFS period, with mounting annual deficits from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget balances at £234.1m, but from 2027/28 onwards the council faces unmet funding gaps: £20.6m (2027/28), £31m (2028/29), and £31.8m (2029/30). These gaps represent 7.9%, 11.3%, and 11.2% of projected expenditure respectively. The council acknowledges this is 'a significant challenge' requiring immediate strategic action from April 2026.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the sustainability of the council's financial position and whether the deficit can be closed through savings without service cuts that damage revenue capacity.
findings.figures: £83.4 million total gap; annual gaps of £20.6m, £31.0m, and £31.8m; funding gaps as % of budget: 7.9%, 11.3%, 11.2%
findings.quote: The projections below, and detailed at Annex B, reflect a funding gap for the medium-term period 2026/27 to 2029/30 of £83.4 million.

findings.headline: External auditor flagged savings delivery as an area requiring improvement in 2024/25
findings.detail: The Annual Auditor's Report published in September 2025 included a key recommendation on DSG deficit management and an improvement recommendation on achievement of savings. This indicates the auditor identified control or delivery issues.
