findings.detail: The council is facing rising cost and demand pressures across adult social care, emergency accommodation, special educational needs, and home-to-school transport. The 2026/27 budget attempts to address these by increasing allocations, but the underlying demand trend remains upward.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's cost estimates reflect genuine underlying demand trends or are based on optimistic assumptions; these service areas are typically persistent pressures that grow with demographics.
findings.figures: £5.6m in-year cost pressures in 2025/26 across these areas
findings.quote: In-year cost pressures represent increases in client demand and complexity of care across adult social care budgets and increases in demand for temporary accommodation in the Community Wellbeing Directorate, pressures in public transport subsidised routes in the Economy & Environment Directorate and continuing budget pressures in SEND and Home to School Transport costs.

findings.paper_title: SUPPLEMENT - S151 Officer Section 25 Report 2026-27 (Appendix G - agenda item 10)
findings.headline: Current year (2025/26) showing £3.7 million forecast overspend after management action
findings.detail: The original Q2 forecast variance of £7.0m has been reduced to £3.7m through management recovery action, but the council is still running over budget. The overspend includes £5.6m of unbudgeted cost pressures and includes the £1.4m of savings targets flagged as at risk.
findings.matters: A lender concerned about financial management needs to see whether current-year budgets are realistic; an overspend even after management action suggests either cost estimating or demand-management issues.
findings.figures: £7.0m initial variance (3.0% of net budget); £3.7m forecast after management action; £5.6m in-year cost pressures
findings.quote: The Quarter 2 revenue outturn position for 2025/26 reports a forecast variance from budget of £7.0 million (3.0% of net budget), before management recovery action which is expected to reduce the forecast overspend to £3.7 million by 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: SUPPLEMENT - S151 Officer Section 25 Report 2026-27 (Appendix G - agenda item 10)
findings.headline: £11.9 million of savings from 2024/25 were not delivered and rolled forward into 2025/26
findings.detail: The council failed to deliver recurrent savings in the prior year and re-profiled them into the current year. Of £15.8m total savings targets monitored for 2025/26, only £14.4m is forecast for delivery with £1.4m remaining 'at risk'. This is a pattern of savings targets not being achieved.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that savings plans are realistic; repeated slippage suggests either the plans are not achievable or service management has struggled with delivery, both of which affect financial forecasts.
findings.figures: £11.9m rolled forward from 2024/25; £15.8m total 2025/26 target; £1.4m assessed as 'at risk'
findings.quote: Savings of £11.9 million not delivered recurrently in 2024/25 were carried forward into 2025/26... with the balance of £1.4 million assessed as 'at risk'.

findings.paper_title: SUPPLEMENT - S151 Officer Section 25 Report 2026-27 (Appendix G - agenda item 10)
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves for budget resilience depleting sharply over two years, from £16.8m to £11.4m
findings.detail: Reserves held for budget resilience are forecast to fall by 32% between March 2025 and March 2027, while liabilities and risk reserves are forecast to fall from £14.1m to £0.1m. This signals the council is burning through contingency to balance the budget.
findings.matters: A lender is concerned when reserves are depleting faster than income growth; this reduces the council's capacity to absorb future shocks and suggests structural budget pressures.
findings.figures: Budget resilience reserves: £16.8m (31 March 2025) to £11.4m (31 March 2027); liabilities and risk reserves: £14.1m to £0.1m
findings.quote: forecast movement in earmarked reserves and reduction in balances held for budget resilience (from £16.8 million at 31 March 2025 to £11.4 million forecast at 31 March 2027) and liabilities and risk (from £14.1 million at 31 March 2025 to £0.1 million forecast at 31 March 2027)

findings.paper_title: SUPPLEMENT - S151 Officer Section 25 Report 2026-27 (Appendix G - agenda item 10)
findings.headline: DSG deficit forecast to reach £37.5 million by March 2026, with statutory override protection ending in 2028
findings.detail: The high needs block deficit is forecast to increase by £17.5m in 2025/26 alone. The council is managing this through a deficit management plan, but the scale of the problem and pending government solution create material uncertainty about the council's reserves when the statutory accounting protection expires.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liability that could materially impact the council's balance sheet and borrowing capacity when the statutory override expires; the council awaits government solution but has no certainty on timing or outcome.
findings.figures: £37.5 million cumulative deficit by March 2026; £17.5 million increase in 2025/26; override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: This remains a significant risk for the council with a forecast deficit at Q2 of 2025/26 of £17.5 million within the High Needs block of the DSG; increasing the cumulative deficit to £37.5 million by 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: SUPPLEMENT - S151 Officer Section 25 Report 2026-27 (Appendix G - agenda item 10)
findings.headline: Central government funding to fall by £17.3 million over the three-year settlement to 2028/29
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 outcome confirms a significant reduction in the council's core spending allocation. This compounds existing budget pressures and reduces financial flexibility when demand for services is rising.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has a structural funding gap it cannot close through efficiency alone; a £17.3m headwind over three years is material to medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £17.3 million reduction over 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.quote: The outcome of the Fair Funding Review 2.0 represents a total reduction in the council's allocation of funding from central government of £17.3 million over the multi-year settlement period from 2026/27 to 2028/29.

findings.headline: Borrowing above corporate limit requires demonstrable revenue savings to cover debt servicing costs, constraining future revenue flexibility
findings.detail: The strategy states that funding above the £6.7m corporate limit is 'available to support capital investment that gives a clear pay back through revenue budget savings.' This means each major capital project must generate internal revenue to service its own debt, reducing the pool of savings available for other pressures or service improvements.
findings.matters: Creates competing claims on future revenue budget; if spend-to-save projects underperform, debt costs still need funding from elsewhere in revenue
findings.figures: Corporate borrowing limit: £6.7m per annum
findings.quote: Funding above the corporate limit of £6.7m is available to support capital investment that gives a clear pay back through revenue budget savings.

findings.headline: Council plans to internally borrow ahead of S106 developer contributions, creating contingent liability if developments fail to trigger payment obligations
findings.detail: The strategy introduces a new approach where the council will internally borrow to fund projects before developer contributions arrive, repaying from S106 funds when received. However, the council acknowledges the risk: 'if the development does not reach the trigger point for payment, the Council would then have to find alternative funding.' This could occur if developments are delayed, scaled back, or become unviable.
findings.matters: Creates unquantified contingent liabilities if developments stall or don't reach trigger points; represents a change to borrowing pattern and adds execution risk
findings.figures: No specific amounts quantified for planned internal borrowing against S106
findings.quote: In future once a S106 has been completed, planning permission has been granted and the development the subject of the agreement has commenced, with the right governance in place the Council will be able to internally borrow to fund the project to commence prior to the developer contributions being received...Do note however there may be a risk to the Council namely, if the development does not reach the trigger point for payment, the Council would then have to find alternative funding.

findings.headline: Council strategy depends critically on continued disposal of surplus property assets to generate capital receipts
findings.detail: The document states 'The disposal of surplus assets is critical to deliver the Councils Capital Strategy.' Current capital receipts reserve stands at £34.8m (end of 2024/25), with the capital programme explicitly using £34.9m from this reserve. The council is undertaking 'a major review of property assets' to identify disposals, but market conditions and property values are not subject to council control.
findings.matters: Reliance on asset sales creates exposure to property market weakness; slower disposal pace would immediately constrain capital programme and force difficult prioritisation decisions
findings.figures: Capital receipts reserve balance: £34.8m at end 2024/25; Programme funded by capital receipts: £34.973m
findings.quote: The disposal of surplus assets is critical to deliver the Councils Capital Strategy. Specifically, the delivery of the property maintenance and office accommodation review requires receipts to fund PB costs...At the end of 2024/25 financial year there was a balance of £34.8m in the capital receipts reserve.

findings.headline: Highways network has c£108.7m backlog in carriageways alone, with total unfunded maintenance backlog estimated at c£200m across all categories
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges that central government grants do not cover capital investment needed to prevent further deterioration. The document provides a detailed breakdown showing carriageways at c£108.7m, structures at c£82.5m, and multiple other asset categories with shortfalls. The council states it 'continues to lobby central government for additional support' but currently funds the gap from revenue.
findings.matters: Unfunded infrastructure liabilities indicate hidden future costs and carry service delivery risk; pressure to address this could constrain revenue in future periods
findings.figures: Carriageways c£108.7m; Structures c£82.5m; Footways and Cycleways c£1.7m; Street Lighting c£1.5m; Traffic Signals c£2.4m; plus smaller categories totalling c£200m+
findings.quote: Like many councils the highways network has deteriorated over time with central government grants not able to cover all the capital investment required to prevent further deterioration of the highway network...Carriageways c£108.7m, Structures c£82.5m

findings.headline: Council is taking additional borrowing beyond its normal £6.7m annual corporate limit to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The document states that the council has approved borrowing above its standard corporate funded limit of £6.7m per annum. Both the Medium-Term Financial Strategy and Treasury Management Strategy have been updated to accommodate this additional borrowing to fund the capital proposals, indicating a material increase in debt servicing obligations.
findings.matters: Higher debt levels reduce financial flexibility and increase revenue budget pressure through higher interest payments, particularly significant if revenues are constrained
findings.figures: £6.7m per annum corporate limit; additional borrowing amount not quantified but treasury strategy updated to include it
findings.quote: Borrowing has always been allowed within the current agreed limits of £6.7m per annum plus any previously approved Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) provision that has not been used...this year additional borrowing is being taken to fund the proposals, both the MTFS and Treasury Management Strategy have included the additional borrowing

findings.headline: Debt servicing costs will rise to 15% of net revenue stream by 2028/29, up from 10% in 2024/25
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs (MRP plus interest payable) to net revenue stream rises from 10% in 2024/25 to 12% in 2026/27, and reaches 15% by 2028/29. This trend shows an increasing proportion of the revenue budget consumed by debt service, squeezing room for service investment and operational flexibility.
findings.matters: Rising financing burden indicates tightening financial flexibility. At 15%, the council approaches levels where debt service materially constrains revenue flexibility and financial stress becomes material. This limits the council's ability to respond to unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: Financing costs as % of net revenue: 10% (2024/25) → 12% (2026/27) → 15% (2028/29); total financing costs £28.5m (2026/27) rising to £35.2m (2028/29)
findings.quote: The calculated ratios of between 10% and 15% confirm that the council's borrowing is currently considered to be affordable.

findings.headline: Total borrowing forecast to increase 66% from £135.5 million to £225.8 million in two years
findings.detail: Current borrowing as at 31 October 2025 stands at £135.5 million, forecast to reach £161.4 million by March 2026 and then jump to £225.8 million by March 2027. The £64.4 million movement in 2026/27 alone comprises £52.2 million for capital programmes and £19.9 million for DSG deficit, offset by £7.7 million principal repayments.
findings.matters: Debt growth of this scale materially increases leverage and financial risk. Lenders assess trajectory and velocity of debt accumulation as a key indicator of financial sustainability and repayment capacity.
findings.quote: The council borrowing is forecast to be £161.4 million at 31 March 2026. This is expected to increase to £225.8 million by 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: £19.9 million of 2026/27 borrowing will fund an increasing Dedicated Schools Grant deficit
findings.detail: The council identifies DSG deficit as a key driver of borrowing requirements alongside capital spend. Of the £64.4 million borrowing increase in 2026/27, £19.9 million is specifically for DSG funding. This represents unfunded liability — not asset-backed borrowing but coverage of a revenue shortfall that the paper indicates is 'increasing' without disclosing the accumulated deficit size.
findings.matters: DSG deficit funding represents structural budget pressure and an unfunded liability. Unlike capital borrowing, it does not generate assets to support repayment, increasing financial risk. A growing deficit signals revenue-side stress that borrowing alone cannot solve long-term.
findings.figures: £19.9 million additional borrowing for DSG in 2026/27; DSG deficit described as 'increasing'
findings.quote: Borrowing requirements are also driven by the increasing Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget, Medium Term Financial and Treasury Management Strategy - Revenue, main report
findings.headline: Sector trend: 50–100 councils expected to seek Emergency Financial Support in 2026/27, up from 30 in 2025/26; 6 of those 30 had issued Section 114 notices
findings.detail: The paper notes that 30 councils received Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) in 2025/26, and 6 of those had previously issued Section 114 notices (virtual bankruptcy notices). The sector is now expecting 50–100 councils to apply for EFS in 2026/27 to balance revenue budgets. The paper notes: 'continuing pressures in costs and demand for services alongside changes in funding allocations mean that the sector is expecting a further increase in requests for support to manage financial pressures.'
findings.matters: This is sector-wide signal of stress. Herefordshire is not unique, but the fact that the number of councils needing government bailout is tripling suggests something structural has broken in local government finance. It raises the question of whether Herefordshire is next.
findings.figures: 30 councils received EFS in 2025/26; 6 of those 30 had previously issued Section 114 notices; 50–100 councils expected to apply for EFS in 2026/27
findings.quote: continuing pressures in costs and demand for services alongside changes in funding allocations mean that the sector is expecting a further increase in requests for support to manage financial pressures

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget, Medium Term Financial and Treasury Management Strategy - Revenue, main report
findings.headline: Children & Young People Directorate has exhausted its planned savings; future years will need to find new cuts from a service already tight
findings.detail: The council approved a 3-year financial plan for Children & Young People in 2024/25 targeting £10.2m savings over 2024/25–2026/27. By the end of 2026/27, the directorate will have delivered £9.78m of these savings, plus a £2.7m underspend in 2024/25. The paper states explicitly: 'Savings requirements in future years in the Children & Young People Directorate will form part of the wider council savings proposals for 2027/28 and onwards, as the savings targets per the original 3 Year Financial Plan have been met.' This means the directorate has no remaining headroom in its planned programme.
findings.matters: The directorate that had a funded 3-year plan is now finished with it, and future savings will need to come from reduced service quality or further headcount cuts in a service that has already had significant restructuring. This is where savings get harder.
findings.figures: Original 3-year plan savings target £10.2m; delivered and proposed through 2026/27 £9.78m; additional underspend 2024/25 £2.7m; no further savings planned beyond 2026/27 from this directorate
findings.quote: Savings requirements in future years in the Children & Young People Directorate will form part of the wider council savings proposals for 2027/28 and onwards, as the savings targets per the original 3 Year Financial Plan have been met.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget, Medium Term Financial and Treasury Management Strategy - Revenue, main report
findings.headline: Savings delivery track record weak: only 56% of 2024/25 savings delivered; 2025/26 showing 51% delivered and 9% at risk
findings.detail: Council approved £19.5m of savings in 2024/25 but only £10.9m (56%) were actually delivered. In 2025/26, at Q2 (September), 51% of savings have been delivered, 40% are on target, and 9% are at risk. The council is now proposing £20m of new savings for 2026/27 while still chasing delivery of old ones. The paper acknowledges: 'Delivery of savings at a time of increasing demand and budget pressures remains a significant challenge for the council.'
findings.matters: Proposed savings cannot be relied upon if the track record of delivery is poor. A lender assessing the sustainability of this budget must assume lower delivery rates than promised, which leaves the council with a larger structural gap.
findings.figures: 2024/25: £19.5m approved savings, £10.9m (56%) delivered; 2025/26 Q2: 51% delivered, 40% on target, 9% at risk; 2026/27: £20.0m new savings proposed
findings.quote: Delivery of savings at a time of increasing demand and budget pressures remains a significant challenge for the council.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget, Medium Term Financial and Treasury Management Strategy - Revenue, main report
findings.headline: Business Rates Pooling ended; loss of £0.7m recurring income due to reset of business rates regime
findings.detail: Herefordshire was part of the Herefordshire and Worcestershire Business Rates Pool, which generated £0.7m annual saving in 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26 by spreading levy risk across multiple authorities. The Business Rates Retention Scheme has been reset as part of the Fair Funding Review. Due to changes to levy and safety net calculations, the pool will not continue in 2026/27. The council loses this recurring income with no offset.
findings.matters: Recurring income that was reliable and recurring is no longer available. This contributes to the structural funding shortfall the council must now close with tax rises and savings.
findings.figures: £0.7 million annual pooling benefit in each of 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26; total accumulated benefit £2.1 million; no pooling benefit in 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: Due to the full reset of the BRRS and changes to levy and safety net calculations, the Herefordshire & Worcestershire Business Rates Pool will not continue in 2026/27 and the council will no longer benefit from pooling gains.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget, Medium Term Financial and Treasury Management Strategy - Revenue, main report
findings.headline: Business Rates Risk Reserve drawn down £3.2m in 2026/27 to fund the Fair Funding Review shortfall, with further draws expected
findings.detail: The Business Rates Risk Reserve held £13.3m at 1 April 2025. The 2026/27 budget draws £3.2m to mitigate the funding loss from the Fair Funding Review. The paper explicitly states: 'It is expected that further use of this reserve may be required over the multi-year Settlement period to manage continuing, further reductions in the council's allocation of funding from Central Government.' This is using a finite, one-off reserve to fund recurring revenue shortfalls.
findings.matters: Reserves exist to absorb shocks. Using them to fund structural budget gaps signals the council cannot balance recurring budgets from recurring income. This weakens resilience and is unsustainable.
findings.figures: Business Rates Risk Reserve balance £13.3m at 1 April 2025; planned draw £3.2m in 2026/27; reserve exists to manage business rates income volatility and appeals
findings.quote: It is expected that further use of this reserve may be required over the multi-year Settlement period to manage continuing, further reductions in the council's allocation of funding from Central Government.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget, Medium Term Financial and Treasury Management Strategy - Revenue, main report
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit ballooning from £20m to £37.5m in one year, with no confirmed government solution when statutory override ends March 2028
findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit brought forward at 1 April 2025 was £20.0m. The Q2 2025/26 forecast shows a £17.5m overspend in the High Needs block, raising the projected cumulative deficit to £37.5m by 31 March 2026. The statutory override that allows councils to hold DSG deficits off-balance-sheet ends 31 March 2028. Government has announced a Schools White Paper early 2026 but the paper notes: 'confirmation of specific arrangements and conditions attached to future support have not yet been provided.' Nationally, the DSG deficit exceeds £6.0 billion and is projected to reach £14.0 billion by end of override.
findings.matters: This is a time-bomb. If government does not extend the override or fund the accumulated deficit, Herefordshire will face a £37.5m+ hit to its revenue budget in 2028, or will be forced to issue a Section 114 notice. The paper admits: 'many local authorities issuing Section 114 notices being unable to set a balanced revenue budget' once the override ends.
findings.figures: DSG cumulative deficit brought forward £20.0m; Q2 2025/26 forecast overspend £17.5m; projected cumulative deficit by 31 March 2026 £37.5m; national sector deficit £6.0 billion rising to £14.0 billion by March 2028
findings.quote: Any deficit not funded through planned SEND reform and support from Central Government will have a significant impact on the council's overall financial position once the override period ends on 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget, Medium Term Financial and Treasury Management Strategy - Revenue, main report
findings.headline: Herefordshire receiving drastically less government funding per resident than urban councils—77% of indexed 2024/25 funding vs 121% for urban authorities by 2028/29
findings.detail: Rural Services Network analysis shows Herefordshire will receive government funding per head of only 77% of 2024/25 indexed levels by 2028/29, whilst urban authorities receive 121%. By 2028/29, most urban councils will have around £100 more spending power per resident than most rural councils. The government's funding formulae place greater weight on urban deprivation factors and ignore remoteness costs, despite evidence submitted by the council and sector bodies.
findings.matters: A rural authority locked into permanently lower grant per capita than urban peers faces a structural disadvantage that cannot be resolved through efficiency. This determines long-term sustainability and may affect credit metrics.
findings.figures: Herefordshire government-funded spending power 77% by 2028/29 vs 121% for urban authorities; most urban councils receiving ~41% more per head in 2026/27; residents in most rural areas paying ~20% more in council tax than most urban residents
findings.quote: Herefordshire's position as drastically disadvantaged by the outcome of the Fair Funding Review (77% by 2028/29)

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget, Medium Term Financial and Treasury Management Strategy - Revenue, main report
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review cuts £17.3m of government grant, forcing maximum council tax increases every year through 2028/29
findings.detail: Herefordshire's allocation of central government funding fell £17.3m following redistribution through the Fair Funding Review, compared to 2025/26. The council now faces maximum annual 3% core council tax rises plus 2% adult social care precept (4.99% total) in each year of the multi-year settlement, because the government's own Core Spending Power calculation assumes these rises will fund the increase. Without them, the council cannot balance the budget.
findings.matters: A council locked into maximum tax rises every year with no discretion signals structural budget stress. Lenders need to know whether the taxpayer base can bear this without political collapse or service cuts deeper than planned.
findings.figures: £17.3 million reduction in central government funding 2026/27; 4.99% council tax increase (2.99% core + 2% adult social care precept); council tax requirement increases from £143.4m (2025/26) to £153.0m (2026/27)
findings.quote: the council is forced to make the maximum permitted increase in each of the MTFS period to ensure delivery of services can be sustained

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Treasury Management Outturn Q2 2025/26
findings.headline: Significant internal borrowing leaves council reliant on cash reserves to fund the capital programme
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement of £320.6m far exceeds its long-term external borrowing of £135.5m. This £185m gap must be funded from day-to-day cash generation and reserves—a position the council describes explicitly: the CFR 'demonstrates that the Council has significant internal borrowing' when compared to actual long-term borrowing.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing depends on sustained revenue cash generation; if income pressures increase (as DSG deficits suggest), or if capital spending continues, the council has limited ability to continue self-funding capital investment
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement £320.6m; long-term external borrowing £135.5m; internal borrowing £185.1m
findings.quote: The council's Capital Financing Requirement at 1st April 2025 is £320.6m, which demonstrates that the Council has significant internal borrowing when compared to the actual long -term borrowing (excluding PFI liabilities) of £135.5m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Treasury Management Outturn Q2 2025/26
findings.headline: Interest payable forecast is overrunning budget by £0.8m and will be covered from reserves
findings.detail: Interest payable on loans is forecast at £6.6m against a budget of £5.8m, an overspend of £0.8m. Combined with a £0.5m underspend on MRP, the net capital financing overspend of £0.3m will be absorbed by drawing on the Treasury Management reserve.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs indicate either higher volumes of borrowing or higher rates (or both); managing this from reserves rather than revenue means less cash available for contingency or service demands
findings.figures: Interest Payable budget £5.8m, forecast £6.6m (overspend £0.8m); total capital financing forecast overspend £0.3m
findings.quote: The overspend will be managed through the use of the Treasury Management reserve.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Treasury Management Outturn Q2 2025/26
findings.headline: DSG deficit is driving significant new borrowing requirement in the second half of the year
findings.detail: The council explicitly expects 'significant further borrowing' in H2 2025/26, citing both capital programme expenditure and the 'ongoing impact of financing the DSG deficit'. The council's current long-term external borrowing is £135.5m against a Capital Financing Requirement of £320.6m, meaning £185m of the capital programme is being funded from internal cash reserves.
findings.matters: DSG deficits represent unfunded statutory pressures on school budgets; councils forced to borrow commercially to finance them face both rising debt and interest costs, reducing financial headroom for other demands
findings.figures: Current long-term borrowing £135.5m; Capital Financing Requirement £320.6m; internal borrowing £185.1m gap
findings.quote: It is anticipated that significant further borrowing will be undertaken in the second half of the financial year, due to actual expenditure within the capital programme and the ongoing impact of financing the DSG deficit.

findings.headline: Overall capital programme reprofiled by £60m, reducing current year spend from £155m to £115m
findings.detail: The council's approved February 2025 budget of £155.2m for 2025/26 has been revised down to £115.1m through reprofiling (moving £60.3m to future years). While £14.5m in additional grants were added, the net effect is a 26% reduction in this year's capital spend. Delays account for £2m and under-budget delivery £949k.
findings.matters: Large-scale reprofiling suggests delivery challenges across the portfolio, not just isolated projects. For a lender, this raises questions about capital discipline, forecasting accuracy, and the council's ability to execute its investment programme on schedule.
findings.figures: Approved budget 2025/26: £155.2m; Revised budget: £115.1m; Reprofiling out: -£60.3m; Additions: +£14.5m
findings.quote: Projects likely to be delayed into 26/27, some with no decisions yet made on spend, others with delays in delivery. -2,038. Project to deliver under budget or not spend full grant allocation -949. -2,987.

findings.headline: HWGTA vocational skills project £2m completely underspent, awaiting business case sign-off
findings.detail: A £2m capital allocation for vocational work-based skills development is forecast at zero spend. The council is 'awaiting the final business case from HWGTA before this project can commence.' This is a full year with no delivery.
findings.matters: A project delivering no activity in its forecast year suggests weak project governance. This matters for lenders assessing whether capital budgets are realistic and whether the council can drive strategic investments.
findings.figures: 2025/26 forecast £0k (budget £2m); 100% variance
findings.quote: We are awaiting the final business case from HWGTA before this project can commence

findings.headline: £2.4m of Education S106 developer contributions on hold with no confirmed delivery timeline
findings.detail: Developer contributions totalling £2.4m earmarked for education have no confirmed spend. Further engagement is required to commission projects, and some projects need to be rescheduled to school holidays. Additional S106 delays across transport and children's services total £3.95m reprofiled.
findings.matters: Developer contributions are expected revenue for capital projects. Large sums on hold signal weak pipeline planning and suggest projects may not materialise. This affects both delivery and the council's ability to rely on this funding source.
findings.figures: £2.4m S106 Education funds on hold; C & F's S106 -£1.55m reprofiled; E & E's S106 -£2.4m reprofiled
findings.quote: Whilst we expect another robust delivery schedule for 2025-2026, our forecasts have been adjusted to reflect our current delivery programme. Further engagement is now required to commission new projects into the 2025-2026 schedule. It's also worth noting that some projects have been rescheduled because they can only be completed during school holidays or non-term periods. Furthermore, £2.4m of S106 Education funds are currently on hold, awaiting suitable timelines to begin on-site delivery.

findings.headline: School capital work at Aylestone delayed by planning permission; Brockhampton works overrunning budget
findings.detail: Two significant school capital schemes are experiencing delays. Aylestone school work has been pushed back due to delayed planning permission. Brockhampton Adaptation works have tendered at over budget, and the school has approached DfE for additional funding before works can start. £6.5m of Basic Needs funding has been reprofiled out of 2025/26.
findings.matters: School capital investment delays affect education delivery and reveal planning/procurement challenges. Cost overruns requiring additional DfE funding indicate budget discipline issues at delivery stage.
findings.figures: Basic Needs Funding reprofiled: -£6.5m from 2025/26; £5m to 2026/27 and £4m to 2027/28
findings.quote: Works were originally expected to commence at Aylestone school ahead of the summer holidays; however, delays in securing planning permission have significantly pushed back the programme timeline.

findings.headline: Shirehall Improvement Works faces procurement delays and cost uncertainty, £2.7m reprofiled
findings.detail: A major council asset project has experienced 'complex and challenging' procurement delays. Contractor appointment was delayed in Q2, and costs remain at estimate rather than contractual commitment. The council notes 'a degree of risk until project costs and programme are moved from estimate status to contractual commitment.' £2.7m has been reprofiled out of 2025/26.
findings.matters: Unresolved cost estimates on a major asset project creates financial uncertainty. This is relevant to any lender assessing the council's capital discipline and ability to deliver projects on budget.
findings.figures: 2025/26 forecast £250k (original budget £2.9m); £2.7m reprofiled to 2026/27
findings.quote: A complex and challenging procurement process has led to some delay to contractor appointment in Q2, but this should be finalised during Q3 so that the final stage of RIBA 4 pre-construction design can begin in earnest, focused on refining and firming up project phasing scopes, costs and programme. A degree of risk until project costs and programme are moved from estimate status to contractual commitment.

findings.headline: Hereford Western Bypass Phase 1 delayed by land acquisition issues, £6.5m reprofiled to future years
findings.detail: The largest single capital project is running significantly behind: only £2.1m forecast to spend in 2025/26 against a £8.6m budget. Design has been deferred to the contractor and land acquisition is delayed. The project is now expected to run from Q4 2025/26 through Q1 2026/27 rather than earlier. Total project cost is £40.3m over five years.
findings.matters: A lender funding this council needs to understand multi-year capital commitments and their delivery risk. Delays on this scale affect borrowing profiles and revenue impacts.
findings.figures: Total project £40.3m; 2025/26 forecast £2.1m (original budget £8.6m); £6.5m reprofiled to 2026/27
findings.quote: Much of the design work has been deferred to the contractor stage as deemed better placed with the contractor and so bulk of spend will take place between Q4 25/26 and Q1 26/27. Securing of land has not been able to be completed as quickly as hoped and is more likely that options agreements will be triggered in Q2 26/27.

findings.headline: Council-wide £7.0m overspend at Q2 (3% of budget) signals potential £14m+ full-year variance
findings.detail: Total council outturn is £238.5m against approved budget of £231.5m, a £7.0m overspend at the halfway point. The overspends are concentrated in uncontrollable, demand-led areas with only modest offsetting underspends.
findings.matters: A 3% overspend halfway through the year indicates potential full-year overspend of £12-15m unless significant corrective action is taken. This materially impacts council reserves, borrowing requirements and budget flexibility.
findings.figures: £7.0m overspend; approved budget £231.5m, Q2 outturn £238.5m

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation and children's residential placements both running over budget
findings.detail: General Fund Housing temporary accommodation is £0.5m over budget, and Children's Services residential placements are £0.5m over budget. Both are demand-driven pressures in services where capacity and cost are difficult to control.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation and children's residential placements are growing cost pressures nationally and indicate deprivation or social need factors in the council's population that may be structural.
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation £0.5m overspend; residential placements £0.5m overspend
findings.quote: £0.5m overspend - General Fund Housing - Temporary Accommodation

findings.headline: SEN and home-to-school transport £1.6m overspend indicates underestimated demand
findings.detail: Residential Services - SEN & Home to School Transport is overspending by £1.6m (budget £12.7m, outturn £14.4m, a 13% variance). This is a demand-driven overspend that appears sticky and difficult to reverse.
findings.matters: Transport costs are difficult to reduce mid-year. A 13% variance on SEN transport at Q2 indicates the council underestimated pupil numbers or complexity in budget setting, and this is unlikely to improve.
findings.figures: £1.6m overspend; budget £12.7m, outturn £14.4m
findings.quote: £1.6m overspend - SEN Transport

findings.headline: £1.4m overspend on prior-year savings plans marked 'at risk' of delivery
findings.detail: The council is reporting a £1.4m overspend on '2024/25 c/fwd outstanding Saving Plans considered at risk of delivery'. This means budget reductions committed in the previous year are not being achieved.
findings.matters: Savings slippage from prior years undermines confidence in budget discipline and medium-term financial planning. It suggests the council's ability to deliver planned cost reductions is compromised, a material control weakness.
findings.figures: £1.4m overspend on prior-year at-risk savings
findings.quote: £1.4m overspend - 2024/25 c/fwd outstanding Saving Plans considered 'at risk' of delivery

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand-driven overspend of £5.0m, the largest single variance
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is overspending by £5.0m due to increased demand for residential, nursing, homecare and personal budgets. The budget was £82.0m but outturn is £87.3m. This is the dominant cost pressure in the council's position.
findings.matters: Adult social care is demand-led and difficult to control mid-year. A £5m variance on an £82m budget (6% overspend) at Q2 suggests sustained cost pressure that may persist through the year, potentially reaching £10m+ for the full year.
findings.figures: £5.0m overspend; Adult Social Care budget £82.0m, outturn £87.3m
findings.quote: £5.0m overspend - Increase in demand for Adult Social Care - Residential, Nursing, Homecare and Personal Budgets

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Updated External Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Unaccounted variances in Capital Financing Requirement and cash flow of £1.8m that management cannot explain
findings.detail: The audit identified an immaterial balancing figure variance of £1.8m in Investing Activities on the cash flow statement that the Council was unable to explain. This variance also appears in the consolidated group cash flow. Related issue in CFR disclosure where £5.4m of road investment financing was incorrectly cumulated in the CFR. Management advised this would be reviewed for 2025/26 closedown.
findings.matters: Unexplained cash flow variances and CFR calculation errors indicate potential weaknesses in capital accounting; unresolved items increase audit risk.
findings.figures: £1.8m unexplained cash flow variance; £5.4m CFR cumulative overstatement from road investment financing treatment
findings.quote: In our Council cash flow testing, we identified a balancing figure variance of £1.8 million in Investing Activities, which the council was unable to explain.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Updated External Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Repeated errors in property valuations from incorrect floor area data in both PPE and investment properties
findings.detail: The audit identified errors in floor area data used by the valuer for both land/buildings and investment properties. This was also identified in prior year and a recommendation made but remains open. Current year testing found overstatement of £4.997m in one investment property that was partially sold but the disposed portion remained in the valuation. Testing also identified patterns of potential errors in PPE valuations from floor area mistakes.
findings.matters: Repeated valuation errors on PPE (£385.7m) and investment property (£53.5m) suggest inadequate controls over data provided to external valuers; material assets remain at risk.
findings.figures: £4.997m adjustment for investment property area error in 2024/25; prior year estimate of potential £1.121m PPE error from floor area issues; PPE total £385.7m, investment property £53.5m
findings.quote: As in the prior year we have identified errors as a result of incorrect areas being used to form the valuations of both land and building asses and investment properties. These errors have resulted in adjustments to the financial statement and are reported on pages 39 and 40. In the prior year we raised a recommendation in respect of this matter and that recommendation remains open.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Updated External Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Ongoing control weaknesses: journals below thresholds lack formal review, spreadsheet-based approvals at risk
findings.detail: No formal review process exists for journals below £2m total value or £250k individual line. Management maintain approval records in a spreadsheet rather than digital ledger system, creating risk of manipulation. These were raised as recommendations in prior year and remain open. The Council's accounting system limitations are acknowledged but controls remain weak.
findings.matters: Weak journal controls increase fraud risk and misstatement risk in financial statements; spreadsheet-based approvals are difficult to audit and vulnerable to manipulation.
findings.figures: Threshold: £2m total or £250k per line; testing found no issues from journals in £225k-£250k range, but control weakness remains
findings.quote: There is no formal review process for journals which fall below £2 million total value, or £250,000 for an individual journal line. The use of a spreadsheet to record the approval of journals presents a risk that this record could be manipulated and the controls could be circumvented.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Updated External Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Prior period adjustment of £16.5m for misclassified DCLG grants that were not properly ring-fenced
findings.detail: The Council received £22.9m of grants from DCLG in 2024/25 which was incorrectly classified as non-ring-fenced despite conditions being attached. Grant income was charged through tax and non-specific grant income when it should have been charged through costs of services. This was a prior year issue too, requiring a £16.5m prior period adjustment.
findings.matters: Misclassification of grant funding affects reported service costs and non-specific income; material prior period adjustments reduce confidence in financial reporting controls.
findings.figures: £22.9m current year misclassification; £16.5m prior year adjustment required
findings.quote: The Authority has received £22.9million of grants from the Department for Communities and Local Government (DCLG) which was incorrectly classified as a non-ring-fenced grant despite there being conditions attached to the grant.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Updated External Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Pension fund asset ceiling reduces net asset of £94.9m to liability of £7.1m under IFRIC 14
findings.detail: The Council recognised a credit to the balance sheet of £102.0 million in respect of an asset ceiling under IFRIC 14, which reduced the £94.9 million net pension asset to a £7.1 million net liability. This is a balance sheet swing of £102m and reflects pension fund restrictions on asset recognition. Small changes in key assumptions (0.1% in discount/inflation rates) produce approximately 1.5% effect on liability.
findings.matters: A £102m adjustment to pension accounting is material to balance sheet strength and debt metrics; sensitivity to rate assumptions matters for financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £94.9m gross asset reduced to £7.1m net liability; £102.0m asset ceiling; 0.1% assumption change = ~1.5% effect on liability
findings.quote: The Authority have recognised a credit to the balance sheet of £102.0 million in respect of an asset ceiling, which has reduced the £94.9 million net asset to a £7.1 million liability.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Updated External Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Significant weaknesses in VFM arrangements mean Council not properly securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness
findings.detail: The auditor identified significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements and concluded they are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. Detailed commentary is in the separate Auditor's Annual Report. This spans the three criteria: improving economy/efficiency/effectiveness, financial sustainability, and governance.
findings.matters: Significant VFM weaknesses are a red flag for lenders about operational and financial management quality; a finance director must understand what specific arrangements have failed.
findings.figures: No quantified impact on specific budgets disclosed in this section.
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Updated External Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Management override of controls identified in Student Accommodation capital project with governance failures
findings.detail: The audit identified management override of expected controls on one capital programme. Approval decisions used outdated viability assessments, there was insufficient segregation of duties, procurement lacked documented rationale, and legal advice was not appropriately escalated. Documentation and audit trails for key decisions were incomplete. The Council and audit team undertook extensive forensic investigation which found no further areas of concern, but this was sufficiently serious to warrant forensic specialist involvement.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the Council has governance failures on major capital projects; a finance director needs to understand control breakdowns at this level of spending.
findings.figures: No specific project value disclosed in this extract, but the issue was significant enough to trigger forensic investigation.
findings.quote: Review of the Student Accommodation project identified management override of expected controls, with approval decisions made using outdated viability assessments, insufficient segregation of duties, procurement lacking a documented rationale, legal advice not escalated appropriately, and documentation and audit trails for key decisions were incomplete.
